title: The Servant’s suffering foretold by Isaiah
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ὁ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι τὰ τοῦ λόγου πάντα Κέλσος ὀνειδίζει τῷ σωτῆρι ἐπὶ τῷ πάθει ὡς μὴ βοηθηθέντι ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς ἢ μὴ δυνηθέντι ἑαυτῷ βοηθῆσαι. παραθετέον ὅτι τὸ πάθος αὐτοῦ ἐπροφητεύετο μετὰ τῆς αἰτίας. ὅτι χρήσιμον ἦν ἀνθρώποις τὸ ἐκεῖνον ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἀποθανεῖν καὶ μώλωπα τὸν ἐπὶ τῷ καταδεδικάσθαι παθεῖν. προείρητο δὲ καὶ ὅτι „συνήσουσιν“ αὐτὸν οἱ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν, παρ᾿ οἷς οὐ γεγόνασιν οἱ προφῆται, καὶ λέλεκτο ὅτι „εἶδος ἄτιμον“ ἐν ἀνθρώποις φαινόμενον ἔχων ὀφθήσεται. οὕτω δ᾿ ἔχει ἡ λέξις· „ἰδοὺ συνήσει ὁ παῖς μου, καὶ ὑψωθήσεται καὶ δοξασθήσεται καὶ μετεωρισθήσεται σφόδρα. ὃν τρόπον ἐκστήσονται ἐπὶ σὲ πολλοὶ, οὕτως ἀδοξήσει ἀπὸ ἀνθρώπων τὸ εἶδός σου, καὶ ἡ δόξα σου ἀπο τῶν ἀνθρώπων. οὕτως θαυμάσονται ἔθνη πολλὰ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ, καὶ συνέξουσι βασιλεῖς τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν· ὅτι οἷς οὐκ ἀνηγγέλη περὶ αὐτοῦ ὄψονται, καὶ οἳ οὐκ ἀκηκόασι συνήσουσι. κύριε, τίς ἐπίστευσε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν; καὶ ὁ βραχίων κυρίου τίνι ἀπεκαλύφθη; ἀνηγγείλαμεν ὡς παιδίον ἐναντίον αὐτοῦ, ὡς ῥίζα ἐν γῇ διψώσῃ· οὐκ ἔστιν εἶδος αὐτῷ οὐδὲ δόξα. καὶ εἴδομεν αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος οὐδὲ κάλλος. ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον καὶ ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ πάντας ἀνθρώπους· ἄνθρωπος ἐν πληγῇ ὢν καὶ εἰδὼς φέρειν μαλακίαν, ὅτι ἀπέστραπται τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ. ἠτιμάσθη καὶ οὐκ ἐλογίσθη. οὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐλογισάμεθα αὐτὸν εἶναι ἐν πόνῳ καὶ ἐν πληγῇ καὶ ἐν κακώσει. αὐτὸς δὲ ἐτραυματίσθη διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, καὶ μεμαλάκισται διὰ τὰς ἀνομίας ἡμῶν· παιδεία εἰρήνης ἡμῶν ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν. τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἡμεῖς ἰάθημεν. πάντες ὡς πρόβατα ἐπλανήθημεν, ἄνθρωπος τῇ ὁδῷ αὐτοῦ ἐπλανήθη· καὶ κύριος παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν. καὶ αὐτὸς διὰ τὸ κεκακῶσθαι οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ· ὡς πρόβατον ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἤχθη, καὶ ὡς ἀμνὸς ἐναντίον τοῦ κείροντος ἄφωνος, οὕτως οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ. ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη· τὴν γενεὰν αὐτοῦ τίς διηγήσεται; ὅτι αἴρεται ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ αὐτοῦ, ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνομιῶν τοῦ λαοῦ μου ἤχθη εἰς θάνατον.“
pass_a_gloss: Since Celsus, professing (ἐπαγγελλόμενος) to know all the things of the word/teaching (λόγου), reproaches (ὀνειδίζει) the Saviour over the suffering (πάθει) as not having been helped (βοηθηθέντι) by the Father or not having been able to help himself, it must be set beside (παραθετέον) that his suffering was prophesied with its cause (αἰτίας): that it was useful (χρήσιμον) for men that he should die on behalf of (ὑπέρ) them and suffer the bruise/weal (μώλωπα) upon being condemned (καταδεδικάσθαι). It had been foretold also that those from the nations 'will understand' (συνήσουσιν) him, among whom the prophets did not arise, and it had been said that he will be seen having 'a dishonoured form' (εἶδος ἄτιμον) appearing among men. The wording (λέξις) runs thus: 'Behold, my servant/child (παῖς) will understand, and will be exalted and glorified and lifted up (μετεωρισθήσεται) exceedingly. As many will be astonished (ἐκστήσονται) at you, so your form will be without glory (ἀδοξήσει) from men, and your glory from men. So many nations will marvel at him, and kings will hold shut (συνέξουσι) their mouth; for those to whom it was not announced (ἀνηγγέλη) about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand. Lord, who believed our report (ἀκοῇ)? And the arm (βραχίων) of the Lord, to whom was it revealed? We announced [him] as a little child (παιδίον) before him, as a root in thirsty earth; he has no form nor glory. And we saw him, and he had no form nor beauty (κάλλος); but his form dishonoured and failing (ἐκλεῖπον) beside all men; a man being in a stroke (πληγῇ) and knowing to bear weakness (μαλακίαν), because his face has been turned away (ἀπέστραπται). He was dishonoured and was not reckoned (ἐλογίσθη). This one bears our sins and is pained (ὀδυνᾶται) for us, and we reckoned him to be in toil (πόνῳ) and in a stroke and in affliction (κακώσει). But he was wounded (ἐτραυματίσθη) for our sins and made weak (μεμαλάκισται) for our lawlessnesses (ἀνομίας); the discipline (παιδεία) of our peace upon him. By his bruise (μώλωπι) we were healed. All as sheep went astray, a man went astray in his way; and the Lord gave him over (παρέδωκεν) to our sins. And he, through having been afflicted (κεκακῶσθαι), does not open his mouth; as a sheep to slaughter he was led, and as a lamb before the one shearing it voiceless (ἄφωνος), so he does not open his mouth. In his humiliation (ταπεινώσει) his judgement (κρίσις) was taken away (ἤρθη); his generation (γενεάν) who will tell (διηγήσεται)? For his life is taken from the earth; from the lawlessnesses of my people he was led to death.'
pass_b_english: Celsus, who professes to know everything about our teaching, reproaches the Saviour over his suffering, as though he had not been helped by the Father or had not been able to help himself. We must therefore show that his suffering was foretold together with its cause: that it was to the profit of mankind that he should die for them and suffer the bruise that came with his condemnation (Isaiah 53:5). It had also been foretold that those from the nations, among whom the prophets had not arisen, "will understand" him (Isaiah 52:15), and it had been said that he would be seen with a "form without honour" in the sight of men (Isaiah 53:3). The text runs thus:

"Behold, my servant shall understand, and he shall be exalted and glorified and lifted up exceedingly. Just as many shall be astonished at you, so shall your form be held in no esteem by men, and your glory by men. So shall many nations marvel at him, and kings shall shut their mouths; for those to whom nothing was announced about him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand" (Isaiah 52:13-15).

"Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced him as a little child before him, as a root in a thirsty land. He has no form nor glory; and we saw him, and he had no form nor beauty. But his form was without honour and fell short of all men's: a man under the stroke, and knowing how to bear weakness, for his face is turned away. He was dishonoured and held of no account. He bears our sins and suffers pain for us, and we reckoned him to be in toil and under the stroke and in affliction. But he was wounded because of our sins and made weak because of our lawless deeds; the chastisement that brings us peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed. All of us went astray like sheep; each man went astray in his own way; and the Lord gave him up for our sins. And he, because he has been afflicted, does not open his mouth. As a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb is silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgement was taken away. Who shall tell of his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth; because of the lawless deeds of my people he was led to death" (Isaiah 53:1-8).

choices.choice: The opening Ἐπεὶ δὲ ... clause is closed in the staged text by a full stop before παραθετέον; read as one sentence ('Since Celsus ... we must show') and rendered as two English sentences. Isaiah 52:13-53:8 is quoted from the Septuagint, and the English follows the Greek, not the Hebrew: e.g. 'my servant shall understand' (συνήσει), 'We announced him as a little child' (ἀνηγγείλαμεν ὡς παιδίον; other Septuagint witnesses read ἀνέτειλε, 'he sprang up'), 'the chastisement that brings us peace' (παιδεία εἰρήνης ἡμῶν), 'the Lord gave him up for our sins' (παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν, dative of cause), 'because of the lawless deeds of my people he was led to death' (ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνομιῶν). Isaiah's verse numbers in these chapters are the same in the Septuagint and English Bibles. The staged text has ἀπο for ἀπὸ in 52:14; no change in sense. ἀδοξήσει ἀπὸ ἀνθρώπων in 52:14 is rendered 'be held in no esteem by men', and εἶδος is 'form' throughout the quotation, as in Origen's lead-in ('form without honour'). 'Suffer the bruising that came with his condemnation' (μώλωπα τὸν ἐπὶ τῷ καταδεδικάσθαι) points to Isaiah 53:5 ('by his bruise we were healed'). The words 'it was to the profit of mankind that he should die for them' may echo John 11:50 or 18:14, but the vocabulary differs (χρήσιμον, not συμφέρει), so they are not cited inline. 'In the sight of men' renders ἐν ἀνθρώποις φαινόμενον. The chapter ends with the quotation; Origen's comment follows in 1.55.
